solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Live on a B road outside English town

blocks.note: kept as it stands
kept as it stands
E = English
RD is the standard abbreviation for road
to be is to live, and 'are' is a form of be

explanation.surface: Someone describes their address: living on a minor road just outside a town in England.
explanation.walkthrough: "English town" wants to be the definition, but ABERDARE is in Wales; English only supplies E, and "on" puts ARE after the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: Aberdare is a town in the South Wales valleys.

clue.text: Hardly occupied with loot

blocks.note: to be at something (at work, at dinner) is to be occupied with it
to rifle a drawer is to ransack or loot it

explanation.surface: A thief is barely busy with the plunder.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay splits after T, but the answer's space falls after A, so the join is disguised.
explanation.definitionFit: "A trifle" means slightly, only a little, as in "a trifle odd", which is close to hardly.

clue.text: Not demanding extra requirement for film

blocks.note: an easy task is not demanding
a rider is an added clause or condition

explanation.surface: A laid-back star with no extra demands for a film shoot.
explanation.walkthrough: Performers' contracts carry riders listing their demands, so the surface quietly plants the second half.
explanation.definitionFit: Easy Rider is the 1969 road movie with Peter Fonda and Dennis Hopper.

clue.text: EU doles willy-nilly: treat for parasites!

indicators.note: willy-nilly means haphazardly, so the letters fall in any order

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 7 letters

explanation.surface: A Eurosceptic jibe: Brussels hands out money at random to spongers.
explanation.walkthrough: "Parasites" in the surface are freeloaders living on EU handouts; in the answer they are lice.
explanation.definitionFit: To delouse is to rid of lice, a treatment for parasites.

clue.text: Informing people of killer dog?

definitions.note: singular, while the answer is plural

blocks.note: to rat is to inform on someone
a ratter is a dog kept to kill rats

explanation.walkthrough: Two senses of ratter: someone who rats on others, and a dog bred to kill rats. The question mark flags the looseness of number.
explanation.definitionFit: To rat is to inform, so ratters are informers; a ratter is also a terrier kept to kill rats.

clue.text: Flirt’s game, drawing out Romeo

indicators.note: drawing something out of a word pulls it away

blocks.note: croquet is the lawn game with hoops and mallets
Romeo is R in the NATO alphabet

explanation.surface: A flirt's gambit is to lure a Romeo out.
explanation.walkthrough: The "’s" is "is": Flirt is game-without-R. Romeo, the lover, is only the letter R.
explanation.definitionFit: To coquet is to flirt, and a coquet is also a flirtatious man.

clue.text: Dim, cold and ultimately dismal: best left unfinished

indicators.note: ultimately points to the last letter of dismal
a word left unfinished loses its final letter

blocks.note: C = cold, as on taps
kept as it stands
last letter of dismal
the elite are the best; ELITE without its last E

explanation.surface: A gloomy verdict on something dark and cold that is best abandoned.
explanation.walkthrough: "And" looks like a link but goes straight into the answer as letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A candlelit room is dimly lit.

clue.text: Brief tremor keeping sextet alert?

definitions.note: "on the qui vive" means alert; the answer alone is the state of watchfulness

indicators.note: a brief word is cut short, so QUIVER loses its R
the tremor keeps the sextet inside it

blocks.note: a quiver is a tremor, shortened to QUIVE
VI is six in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: A small shiver runs through six musicians waiting to come in.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark covers the stretch: the phrase is usually "on the qui vive", meaning on the alert.
explanation.definitionFit: Qui vive, from a French sentry's challenge, is a state of watchful alertness.

clue.text: Lots of praise for smashing United goalie

indicators.note: smashed letters break apart and reassemble in a new order

blocks.note: U = United, as in football team names
anagram fodder

explanation.surface: A match report: the United goalkeeper is showered with praise for a great display.
explanation.walkthrough: "Smashing" reads as "excellent" in the surface, but it breaks up the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Eulogia is the plural of eulogium, a eulogy, so lots of praise.

clue.text: Being very firm — or cracking?

blocks.note: firmness of purpose, a noun
cracking a problem means solving it; read as a noun

explanation.walkthrough: The dash and question mark suggest a person either staying strong or breaking down; "cracking" is really the solving of a problem.
explanation.definitionFit: Resolution is firmness of purpose, and also the solving (cracking) of a problem or puzzle.

clue.text: Quickly shifting the blame — in vain

indicators.note: shifting the blame moves it off, taking those letters away

blocks.note: rapidly means quickly
to take the rap is to take the blame

explanation.surface: Someone passes the buck fast, and it gets them nowhere.
explanation.walkthrough: The blame is the rap you take; shift it off RAPIDLY and the answer is left.
explanation.definitionFit: Idly can mean to no purpose, as in threats made idly, which is in vain.

clue.text: Saying what will be unusual if not urgent about measure

indicators.note: unusual letters are not in their usual order
the rearranged letters go about, around, the measure

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 11 letters
an ell is an old measure of cloth length

explanation.surface: Advice about triage: something odd is worth noting unless it is urgent.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram gives FORTUNE-T-ING, and ELL drops in after the T.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain paraphrase: a fortune-teller's trade is foretelling the future, which the clue puts as saying what will be.

clue.text: Boring maybe, with no goals

blocks.note: something that never stops can be tedious
an end is a goal or aim, and -less means without

explanation.walkthrough: The second half is really END-LESS: an end is a goal or aim, so something with no goals is endless. "Maybe" signals that endless things are only sometimes boring.
explanation.definitionFit: Something endless may well be boring, and without ends (goals) it is literally end-less.

clue.text: Ceases to accept deliveries incurring delays getting there?

blocks.note: to cease is to stop
in cricket an over is a set of six deliveries (balls) from one bowler

explanation.surface: A courier firm stops taking parcels, and the post is held up.
explanation.walkthrough: The deliveries are cricket balls, not parcels: an over is six balls bowled in a row.
explanation.definitionFit: A stopover is a break in a journey, which delays arrival; the question mark admits it is not a strict synonym.

clue.text: US singer’s term coined for foul-mouthed radio presenter?

definitions.text: term coined for foul-mouthed radio presenter?
definitions.note: a punning description rather than a synonym

blocks.note: a North American songbird, not a pop star

blocks.clueFragment: term coined for foul-mouthed radio presenter?
blocks.note: blue = obscene, and a DJ is a deejay

explanation.surface: A pop star has had a nickname invented about a sweary DJ.
explanation.walkthrough: The singer is a songbird, not a pop star. Blue means obscene, and a DJ (deejay) is a radio presenter, so a smutty one could be called a "blue jay".
explanation.definitionFit: The blue jay is a North American songbird, so a US singer.

clue.text: Appear suddenly surprised by clues, for starters!

definitions.note: the answer is a noun, the things used for starting cars

blocks.note: to jump is to start in sudden surprise
a lead is a clue in an investigation

explanation.surface: A solver jumps as the clues give up their answers, at least the first few.
explanation.walkthrough: "For starters" looks like a first-letters signal, but it is the definition: jump leads start a car.
explanation.definitionFit: Jump leads are the cables used to start a car from another battery, so they are for starters.

clue.text: Delivery coming down from Scottish town, that is leaving before work

indicators.note: the letters of "that is" leave the town name

blocks.note: Airdrie is a town east of Glasgow
i.e. is Latin id est, that is
OP = opus, a work

explanation.surface: A parcel comes down from a Scottish town, and someone departs before the working day.
explanation.walkthrough: "Leaving" reads as someone setting off for the office, but it removes letters; "before work" then places the town remnant ahead of the opus.
explanation.definitionFit: An airdrop is supplies delivered by parachute from an aircraft, a delivery coming down.

clue.text: State home a charity set up

indicators.note: in a down clue, set up means raised, read from bottom to top

blocks.note: to be in is to be at home
a and an are the same article
aid is charitable help

explanation.surface: A government founds a charity and a care home.
explanation.walkthrough: Only "a charity" is turned upside down; IN stays at the top.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Indiana is one of the fifty US states, in the Midwest, capital Indianapolis.

clue.text: Talk over ways to speak ill of

blocks.note: to dis (diss) someone is to disrespect them
to cuss someone is to curse or abuse them

explanation.surface: A debate about how best to insult someone.
explanation.walkthrough: "Ways" is plural because it supplies two words meaning speak ill of, one after the other.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, both verbs: talking a matter over and discussing it are the same act.

clue.text: Struggle to get words out of Frenchwoman in leading role

indicators.note: the Frenchwoman is put in the role

blocks.note: the star plays the leading role
Mme is the abbreviation of Madame

explanation.surface: An English actor cast as a Frenchwoman struggles to get the lines out.
explanation.walkthrough: The Frenchwoman is only the abbreviation MME, which splits STAR after its A.
explanation.definitionFit: A descriptive definition of the verb: a stammerer halts and repeats sounds while trying to speak.

clue.text: Hot air from teacher and officers meeting Heads?

indicators.note: two officers meeting head to head face each other, so one of them is turned round

blocks.note: pupils call a male teacher sir
CO = commanding officer
a second commanding officer

explanation.surface: Staff meetings with head teachers are all hot air.
explanation.walkthrough: "Hot air" suggests empty talk, but here it is a real wind. OC and CO meet at their heads, the C of each.
explanation.definitionFit: The sirocco is a hot wind blowing from North Africa across the Mediterranean.

clue.text: Rank “two star”, being most pessimistic

indicators.note: rank means rotten, so the letters are spoiled into a new order

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 7 letters

explanation.surface: A reviewer awards a mere two stars, taking the gloomiest view.
explanation.walkthrough: "Rank" pretends to mean a grade, which suits the star rating, but it is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: "At worst" is what you say when taking the most pessimistic view.

clue.text: Director of football’s getting promotion

blocks.note: RU = rugby union, a football code, plus 's
a sell is a sales pitch, as in the hard sell

explanation.surface: A football club's director is being moved up.
explanation.walkthrough: "Director of football" is a real club job, which hides that the director is a film-maker. Rugby is football in the sense of rugby football.
explanation.definitionFit: Ken Russell was an English film director (Women in Love, Tommy).

clue.text: Lively music, I agree, and singular — we weren’t bored in vain!

blocks.note: disco is upbeat dance music
"very well" is a way of saying I agree
S = singular, in grammar

explanation.surface: Someone at a lively party insists they were never bored.
explanation.walkthrough: "Bored" means drilled, not weary: the wells speak for themselves, glad their drilling struck something.
explanation.definitionFit: A discovery well is the first well to find oil or gas in a new field, so it was not bored in vain.

clue.text: Regularly visited retired bushman on island

indicators.note: visiting regularly calls at every other letter
to retire is to go back, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: the even letters of BUSHMANON

explanation.surface: A retired outback dweller often drops in on an island.
explanation.walkthrough: "On" looks like a link to the definition but is part of the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Oahu is the Hawaiian island that holds Honolulu.

clue.text: Former champion to consider touring British compound

blocks.note: ex = former
an ace is a champion performer
to rate is to consider or regard
B = British

explanation.surface: A retired champion thinks about a tour of a British camp.
explanation.walkthrough: "Compound" reads as a noun, an enclosure, but it is the verb: to compound a problem is to make it worse.
explanation.definitionFit: To compound a difficulty is to worsen it, which is to exacerbate it.

clue.text: Bone set as rust forms

indicators.note: letters set are put into a new arrangement, as a bone is set back into place

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 6 letters

explanation.surface: A broken bone is set while rust forms, perhaps on the metal pins.
explanation.walkthrough: "Set" reads as a doctor setting a broken bone, but it tells you to rearrange AS RUST.
explanation.definitionFit: The tarsus is the group of bones in the ankle.

clue.text: Steroid used by escort is Olympian’s

indicators.note: the word is used, contained, in the phrase that follows

blocks.note: esCORT IS OLympian's

explanation.surface: A doping scandal: an Olympian's escort was found using steroids.
explanation.walkthrough: The drugs-in-sport surface makes "steroid" feel like a banned substance, but cortisol is one the body makes itself.
explanation.definitionFit: Cortisol is a steroid hormone made by the adrenal glands.
